newsitem.title: USA: Gillette sees second half growth picking up. [CORRECTED 21:21 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Gillette sees second half growth picking up. [CORRECTED 21:21 GMT]

text.p: Gillette Co officials told analysts that growth would pick up in the second half of 1997 while the first half of the year would be slower.

Instead, Investor Relations Vice President Everett Howe said they should look to the second half of the year, when results should show double-digit improvements after the introduction of new products for all the company's lines -- blades and razors, oral hygiene, Braun appliances, and stationery items.
Net income is "not going to be as robust in the second quarter as it will be in the second half," Howe said.
He attributed a sharp decline in sales of stationery products to a combination of weak European economies and consolidations within the office products category.
(Corrects to remove reference to Staples Inc and Office Depot Inc and to clarify that the company made no mention of the possible merger of Staples and Office Depot).

"When you have consolidations, these things happen," Howe said. "So I think once we're by this -- and we are, unless somebody else decides they're going to consolidate --... we'll find that that (stationery products) will get back on track."
Howe said the economies in five of the top 11 markets for Gillette -- France, Germany, Japan, Mexico and Argentina -- were also impeding performance.

Gillette Chief Executive Officer Alfred Zeien told stockholders earlier at the company's annual meeting that "the recent strengthening of the U.S. dollar negatively impacted our sales growth rate by about three percentage points. Our growth rate would have been nine percent instead of six percent if the dollar hadn't strengthened."

Boston-based Gillette, which reported sales of $2.18 billion in the first quarter, up from $2.06 billion for the same period a year earlier, also raised its quarterly dividend by 19 percent to $0.215 per common share, payable June 5 to stockholders of record on May 1.
But shareholders at the annual meeting seemed unimpressed with the dividend hike.
Instead, they asked Zeien about splitting the stock, which was trading down 3-1/8 points to 78-3/4 in latge afternoon.

Zeien, noting the stock has had two-for-one splits twice since 1991 when it had previously reached the $70-a-share range, told the shareholders, "I would expect the board will consider (it) again in the future."
